new.headline: Skip the Wednesday 16-miler: the fitness is built, and the heavy legs are fatigue clearing. Run about 15 easy miles with one short marathon-pace session, then start Sunday at 8:45 to 8:50 and settle at 8:35.

flags.title: Start slower than goal pace
flags.detail: Run miles 1 to 3 at 8:45 to 8:50, then settle at 8:35. Taper legs and a crowd make early miles feel easy, and time banked early costs more in the last 10K.

flags.title: Wednesday pace work
flags.detail: Two marathon-pace miles only. If the first one feels hard, switch to easy running and finish the run. Nothing is gained by pushing four days out.

flags.title: Heavy, flat legs
flags.detail: This is expected after a 46-mile week and a 20-miler. Nothing hurts now. If pain or illness shows up this week, see a doctor or physio rather than testing it on a run.

flags.title: Thursday night sleep
flags.detail: Sleep averaged 7.5 hours last week. Nerves often wreck the night before a race, so a full night on Thursday is the one that counts.

answers.question: Is it crazy to do one more 16-miler on Wednesday so I feel ready?
answers.answer:
Skip it. A 16-miler on Wed Oct 14 would leave you tired on Sunday and add no fitness, because a long run needs one to two weeks to turn into race fitness while its fatigue lasts several days.

Your build is already done: 20 miles on Sep 13 and Oct 4, 17 on Sep 27 and 15 on Sep 20. The heavy, flat legs are that load clearing out, and they often lift in the last two or three days before the race.

For the readiness you are after, Wed Oct 14 includes 2 miles at marathon pace inside a 5-mile run. That is enough to feel goal pace again without paying for it on Sunday.

new.analysis:
Last week went exactly to plan: every run was done at the planned distance, both rest days were real rest, and pain stayed at 0/10 all week. The 34 miles were about a quarter less than the 46 the week before, which is the right size of cut for the first step of a two-week taper. Time in the easy zones was 67.5%, which is normal for a week with one session.

Feeling flat and nervous is a normal taper response, not lost fitness. Fatigue clears in days, while fitness fades over weeks. Your own numbers show nothing slipping: easy pace has held at 9:51 to 9:52 per mile at 139 bpm for four weeks, and last Wednesday's 4 marathon-pace miles came in at 8:36 with no fade.

Race week keeps one short sharpener and a lot of rest. Putting two goal-pace miles four days out leaves time to clear them before the start. About 15 miles of running before the race is far below anything in your recent weeks, and that is the point.

Under 3:45 means 8:35 per mile for 26.2 miles, and your training says that pace is within reach. You held 8:30 to 8:40 for 7 miles on Sep 30, though that took real effort and your heart rate drifted up 17 bpm. The unknown is the last 10K, so the first half should feel almost too easy.

Your heart rate will read high from nerves in the early miles. Go by pace and feel for the first 5 miles, and keep fuel and kit to what you have already used on your long runs.
